title: Relative Velocity
short: Velocities add as vectors when you change reference frames: boats in rivers, planes in wind.
trouble: Students add the river's speed to the boat's speed when the boat heads straight across.

blocks.html: A velocity is always measured relative to something. Walking at $1.5\ \text{m/s}$ on a moving walkway, you move faster relative to the floor than relative to the walkway. When frames move relative to each other, velocities combine by Adding Vectors by Components.

$$\vec{v}_{\text{object, ground}} = \vec{v}_{\text{object, medium}} + \vec{v}_{\text{medium, ground}}.$$ For a boat: its velocity relative to the shore is its velocity relative to the water plus the water's velocity relative to the shore.

In one second, the water carries the boat some distance downstream while the boat moves through the water in the direction it points. Its total displacement relative to the shore is the sum of the two, so its velocity is too. Because the two motions add as vectors, a current at right angles to the boat's heading doesn't help or hinder the crossing; it only moves the boat sideways.

blocks.name: ph-vectors

opts.task: Change the heading. Find the heading that lands the boat straight across. What happens to the crossing time?

blocks.cap: A boat crossing a 60 m river. Pointing straight across, it takes 20 s and drifts 30 m downstream.

blocks.title: Along a line
blocks.q: A plane flies at $220\ \text{km/h}$ relative to the air into a $40\ \text{km/h}$ headwind. What is its ground speed?

blocks.title: Straight across a current
blocks.q: A boat that moves at $4\ \text{m/s}$ in still water points straight across a $60\ \text{m}$ river flowing at $3\ \text{m/s}$.
steps: Crossing time uses only the across part: $t = \dfrac{60}{4} = 15\ \text{s}$.

blocks.title: Aiming upstream
blocks.q: Same boat and river. At what angle from straight across must the boat point to land directly opposite?
steps: The upstream part of its velocity must cancel the current: $4\sin\theta = 3$.
Its across speed is now $4\cos 48.6^\circ \approx 2.65\ \text{m/s}$, so the crossing takes about $22.7\ \text{s}$, longer than before.

blocks.html: Adding the river's speed to the boat's speed when the boat points straight across ("$4 + 3 = 7\ \text{m/s}$, so it crosses faster"). The current is perpendicular to the heading, so it adds as a vector: it changes where the boat lands, not how long it takes to cross. Check: crossing time = width ÷ (the across part of the velocity).
